About: Feynman Diagram Sandbox

Concept
Every piece of a Feynman diagram is a factor in the quantum amplitude: two QED vertices (−ieγμ) and one virtual-photon propagator (−i gμν/q², with q² = s) build M for e⁻e⁺ → μ⁻μ⁺. The spin-averaged ⟨|M|²⟩ = e⁴(1 + cos²θ) carries no s at all — the propagator's 1/s² is cancelled by the s² coming from the spinor currents. The 1/s of the cross section comes from the flux × phase-space factor: dσ/dΩ = ⟨|M|²⟩/(64π²s) ⇒ σ = 4πα²/3s, multiplied by the threshold factor β(3−β²)/2 with β = √(1 − 4mf²/s). So s·σ = (4πα²/3)(ħc)² = 86.85 nb·GeV² is constant in √s (massless limit): reference anchors are 86.85 nb at √s = 1 GeV, 9.650 nb at 3 GeV and 0.869 nb at 10 GeV. Each vertex conserves charge and every lepton family number (colour and baryon number are trivial for leptons). Validity: leading-order QED, one s-channel γ*, fixed α = 1/137.036, massless beams, √s ≪ MZ (no Z exchange, no γ–Z interference, no hadronic resonances). An e⁻e⁺ final state (Bhabha) also has a t-channel diagram, so only the s-channel piece is quoted; τ⁺τ⁻ opens at √s ≥ 2mτ = 3.554 GeV.
Serves
Intro particle physics / QED lectures — first contact with Feynman rules, conservation laws at vertices, and collider cross sections.
Inquiry
Build diagrams yourself: choose a topology (annihilation vs exchange), an exchanged boson (γ / Z⁰ / W± / g), and drag particles onto the legs — every vertex is checked and every failure names its rule. Five puzzles ask for the lowest-order diagram of a given process (one needs BOTH topologies). Commit a prediction for what doubling √s does to σ — σ stays hidden until you do.
Misconception
"More collision energy makes annihilation more likely." It does the opposite: σ ∝ 1/s, so doubling √s quarters σ. Not because the amplitude shrinks — ⟨|M|²⟩ = e⁴(1 + cos²θ) is energy-independent — but because the flux × phase-space factor 1/(64π²s) falls. The "×4" chip encodes the wrong intuition; choosing it draws a dashed ×4 ghost marker that the measured point then contradicts.

Guided Inquiry

1 · Why this topology?

Let’s start with a classic. e⁻e⁺ → μ⁻μ⁺ is drawn as annihilation through a virtual photon. Could the same process go by exchanging a photon instead, while both particles fly on? What do you think?

2 · What crosses?

Now try a different pair. e⁻ and μ⁻ are both matter and different species, so they can’t annihilate — instead they scatter by exchanging a virtual photon. Does anything you could observe actually travel between the vertices?

3 · Could you catch the γ*?

Now back to annihilation. There, the internal photon has q² = s, but every real photon has q² = 0. So could a detector placed between the beams register this photon? What’s your guess?

4 · What can the W do?

Now let’s bring in the W. A neutrino becomes a charged lepton at one vertex, and the reverse happens at the other. Photons, Z bosons and gluons can’t do this — so why do you think the W can?

5 · Two legal diagrams

Here’s a twist. For e⁻e⁺ → e⁻e⁺, both annihilation and exchange are legal: species survive exchange, and particle plus antiparticle can annihilate. So what do you think nature does with two legal diagrams?

6 · Why does σ fall?

One last question. Every diagram evaluates to one measurable number: the cross section σ. If you double √s from 3 to 6 GeV, what do you think happens to σ — and why?

The Physics

Feynman diagrams · what this sim shows, the physics behind it, and every control

01

At a glance

A Feynman diagram is a picture of one term in the quantum amplitude for a process. This sandbox checks every vertex you build and, for e⁻e⁺ → ℓ⁻ℓ⁺, turns the diagram into a cross section σ.

What you'll learn

  • What the lines, the vertices and the time direction of a diagram stand for.
  • Which vertices are allowed, and which boson each process needs.
  • How two diagrams for the same process combine.
  • How σ for e⁻e⁺ → μ⁻μ⁺ depends on √s, and why.
Time runs left to right. Two particles come in, two go out, and a boson line joins the vertices.

What's on screen

  • Legs and slots: two incoming particles on the left, two outgoing on the right, coloured by species (e blue, μ amber, τ purple).
  • Vertices V₁, V₂ and the wavy line: the exchanged boson, labelled with its q². A dashed "now" line sweeps across.
  • Status chip (top right): ✓ when every vertex is allowed, ✗ with the failed rule, amber when √s is too low.
  • Result panel and σ(√s) plot: σ, s·σ, and σ against √s on log axes.
See itLoad the default build, e⁻e⁺ → μ⁻μ⁺. Watch for: dots running in along the legs, the dashed line sweeping across, and a green ✓ in the status chip.

03

A diagram is a recipe for an amplitude

Each piece of the diagram stands for one factor in the amplitude 𝓜 of the process, and the factors multiply:

The amplitude of e⁻e⁺ → μ⁻μ⁺ through a γ*.
  • Legs are the particles that go in and come out. Each gives one spinor (u, v̄ and so on).
  • Vertices V₁ and V₂ each give one coupling factor. For a photon it is −ieγμ.
  • The wavy line is the boson's propagator, −i gμν/q², where q is the momentum it carries.

There are two topologies. In annihilation the incoming pair meets at V₁ and the boson carries everything to V₂. In exchange each incoming particle continues as an outgoing one, and the boson passes momentum between them.

Annihilation (top) and exchange (bottom), with the sim's leg colours.
See itBuild annihilation, e⁻e⁺ → μ⁻μ⁺. Watch for: the incoming pair meeting at V₁, and the wavy line carrying everything across to V₂.
See itBuild exchange, νμe⁻ → μ⁻νe. Watch for: both fermion lines running straight through, joined by a vertical wavy line.
04

Each vertex follows a coupling rule

Before it writes ✓, the sandbox checks both vertices against these rules:

The rules the sandbox applies at a vertex.
  • A γ, Z⁰ or g line does not change species. An e⁻ cannot become a μ⁻ at a photon vertex.
  • Only the W changes species, and only between doublet partners. It carries the charge away: νμ → μ⁻ emits a W⁺.
  • The W emitted at one vertex must be the one absorbed at the other. The sandbox flags a mismatch with ✗.
Left: allowed. Middle: a photon cannot turn e⁻ into μ⁻. Right: a W links doublet partners.

Real W vertices also mix quark generations. The sandbox leaves this out.

See itBuild e⁻e⁺ → μ⁻μ⁺ by exchange with a photon. Watch for: a red ✗ at V₁ and a status chip that names the rule it broke.
See itBuild νμe⁺ → μ⁻ν̄e through a W. Watch for: a red ✗ saying the emitted W does not match the one absorbed.
05

Diagrams are terms, not events

The wavy line is an internal line, and its q² is fixed by the legs. A real photon has q² = 0. The internal line never does.

q² of the internal line in each topology.

Nothing observable travels between the vertices. The line is a factor in 𝓜, not a particle on a path.

When the same legs fit two diagrams, as in e⁻e⁺ → e⁻e⁺, nature adds the amplitudes first and squares the sum:

The cross term belongs to neither diagram alone.

Treating the diagrams as two separate events and adding probabilities would leave out the interference. In the sandbox, σ for e⁻e⁺ → e⁻e⁺ is the s-channel piece only, and the plot header says so.

See itBuild e⁻μ⁻ → e⁻μ⁻ by photon exchange. Watch for: the label on the wavy line reading q² < 0.
See itBuild e⁻e⁺ → e⁻e⁺ by annihilation, then by exchange. Watch for: the status chip staying green ✓ when the topology changes.
06

The cross section falls as 1/s

For e⁻e⁺ → μ⁻μ⁺ through one γ*, the squared amplitude averaged over spins is e⁴(1 + cos²θ), with no s in it. The 1/s comes from the flux and phase-space factor:

In the massless limit. θ is the angle between the μ⁻ and the e⁻ beam.
  • The propagator's 1/s² is cancelled by the factors of s in the spinor currents. It is not the source of the fall.
  • So σ drops by 4 each time √s doubles. In the massless limit s·σ = 86.85 nb·GeV², a constant.
  • The plot labels the massless values 86.85, 9.65 and 0.87 nb at √s = 1, 3 and 10 GeV. The μ mass changes the 1 GeV value by under 0.1%.
See itSweep √s from 1 to 10 GeV with the σ plot open. Watch for: σ falling by a factor of 100 while s·σ barely moves.
07

Mass sets a threshold

A final pair of mass m adds a factor to σ. Here β is the speed of each produced particle in the centre-of-mass frame, in units of c:

The cross section the sandbox reports, in nanobarns.
  • Below √s = 2m, no real pair can be made. σ = 0 and the sandbox calls the channel closed. The diagram itself is still legal.
  • Above it, σ climbs steeply, then joins the 1/s line as β → 1. At 10 GeV, τ⁻τ⁺ is within 1% of it.
  • In the sim's range (0.5–30 GeV) only τ⁻τ⁺ has a threshold, at 2mτ = 3.554 GeV.
√s out

These sliders move the sim too.

σ(√s) from the sim's own formula. τ⁻τ⁺ (violet) joins the μ⁻μ⁺ line above its threshold.
See itBuild e⁻e⁺ → τ⁻τ⁺ at 3 GeV, then raise √s to 6 GeV. Watch for: σ reading 0 below 3.554 GeV, then rising from zero.
08

Where it matters

  • The yardstick at e⁺e⁻ colliders. σ = 4πα²/3s is the reference cross section for pair production. Measured rates for e⁺e⁻ → hadrons are quoted as a ratio R to it.
  • Luminosity. Bhabha scattering, e⁻e⁺ → e⁻e⁺, is common and precisely calculable, so colliders use it to measure how many collisions they delivered.
  • Inverse muon decay. νμe⁻ → μ⁻νe, the W-exchange diagram in the sim, is observed in neutrino beams. It needs a neutrino energy above about 10.9 GeV to make the μ⁻ from an electron at rest.
Go deeper: what the sandbox leaves out
  • R. At lowest order, R = 3 Σ q² over the quarks that can be made, which is 10/3 for u, d, s and c. Measured values lie a little higher because of gluon radiation.
  • The Z⁰. The σ formula has only a photon. The Z⁰ matters near 91 GeV, far above the sim's 30 GeV maximum.
  • α runs. The sim fixes α = 1/137.036. Near the Z⁰ mass it is about 1/129.
09

Summary

In one line. A diagram is a recipe for one term of an amplitude, the vertex rules decide which diagrams exist, and for e⁻e⁺ → ℓ⁻ℓ⁺ the result is σ = 4πα²/3s times a threshold factor.

Key points

  • Legs, vertices and the wavy line each stand for a factor in 𝓜.
  • γ, Z⁰ and g keep the species. Only the W changes it, between doublet partners.
  • When two diagrams fit the same legs, add the amplitudes before squaring.
  • σ ∝ 1/s comes from flux and phase space, and a pair of mass m needs √s > 2m.

Common mix-ups

  • "The wavy line is a photon travelling between the particles." It is off shell and exists only inside the amplitude.
  • "Two diagrams for one process are two separate events." They are two terms of one amplitude, and they interfere.
  • "σ falls because the photon propagator weakens." Its 1/s² is cancelled. The 1/s comes from flux and phase space.

Things to try on your own

  • Solve all five puzzles, finding both diagrams for e⁻e⁺ → e⁻e⁺.
  • Build e⁻e⁺ → τ⁻τ⁺ and step √s across 3.554 GeV.
  • With the plot open, multiply σ by s at 1, 3 and 10 GeV and compare the three products.
